title: British species for green woodwork
subtitle: Which trees to seek out and what each is good for
excerpt: Not all trees suit green woodwork equally. This article covers the main British species used in traditional trades: ash, hazel, sweet chestnut, oak, willow, and sycamore, including how to identify each, what it is used for, and how to source it.

glossaryTerms.definition: A managed woodland system where trees are cut to the stump on a rotation, producing multiple straight stems from each stool. Hazel is the most common coppiced species in Britain.
Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.

content.text: Six British tree species do most of the work in traditional green woodwork: ash, hazel, sweet chestnut, oak, willow, and sycamore. All grow quickly in managed woodland; most come from
coppice
. This article covers the six most useful species for
green wood
hand-tool work.
Ash (Fraxinus excelsior)

The first-choice all-round green-woodwork species. Ash rives cleanly, shaves fast, steam-bends well, and dries straight. The grain is coarse and open; the surface requires more work than sycamore to achieve a fine finish, but for structural pieces (chair legs, rake handles, tool handles), no British species matches it. Ash is currently threatened by ash dieback (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus) in many parts of Britain, which affects future supply from managed woodland. Source from reputable timber merchants or from tree surgeons removing infected trees.
Hazel (Corylus avellana)

The most commonly coppiced species in Britain. Hazel grows in multi-stem stools and produces straight, lightweight poles on a seven to ten year rotation. It splits and shaves easily in the green state, bends reasonably well when young, and dries quickly. It is the material for basket stakes, hurdle uprights, walking sticks, and any project that needs a long, light, straight pole. Smaller-diameter poles (8 to 12 mm) are used as basket weaving rods; larger (25 to 40 mm) for stakes and handles.
Sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa)

The main coppiced species in Kent and Sussex, grown on a twelve to fifteen year rotation for cleft fencing and hop poles. Sweet chestnut is highly durable in the ground (more so than oak in many conditions) because of its high tannin content. It rives along the rays very cleanly and is much straighter in the grain than oak. The grain is coarser than ash and the wood is lighter in weight. A good species for stakes, fencing, and tool handles when ash is not available.
Oak (Quercus robur / petraea)

The prestige British hardwood. Rives along its medullary rays to produce quarter-sawn slats with striking ray figure. Used for basket-weaving slats, shingles (roof tiles), wattle in wattle-and-daub, and cleft lath for furniture. Hard to carve with a knife; requires the axe and drawknife for bulk work. The tannins react with iron tools; use stainless-steel or non-ferrous tools for the best surface quality on oak.
Willow (Salix spp.)

Grown specifically for basket-making from cultivated stools on a one-year pollard cycle. Willow rods (withies) are long, thin, and highly flexible in the green or soaked-dry state. They are the material for virtually all British basket weaving. Willow is not a timber for structural green woodwork: the stems are too thin for most tools-handle or furniture applications. The relevant variety for basket work is buff willow (steamed to tan the bark) or brown willow (unpeeled dried rod); white willow is peeled and dried. Covered in detail in the basketry-willow sub-category.
Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus)

A non-native species that has naturalised very widely in Britain. Fine-grained, food-safe, pale, and carves cleanly in the green state. Used in the dairy and kitchen tradition (butter pats, spoons, boards) because its closed grain resists tainting and it takes a fine knife finish. The grain can be wavy (fiddleback figure) which complicates knife direction; the two-stroke test (see grain-reading article) is important on sycamore. Available from tree surgeons year-round as it is removed from gardens and urban sites regularly.
Sourcing green wood in Britain
Tree surgeons: the most accessible source of urban hardwoods. Ask for rounds from healthy trees, specify the species, and collect within a week of cutting.
Coppice woodland: many coppice groups sell green material directly. The Coppice Association has a directory of managed coppice woodlands.
Specialist green-woodwork suppliers sell billets and rounds for hand-tool work.
Timber merchants: some sell green timber. Ask for material at over 25 per cent moisture content, not kiln-dried.
